title: 30-Day Training Plan
goal: Your kid trains for 30 days toward one thing their body can't do yet: run 2 km without stopping, hold a plank for a minute, swim a length or land a cartwheel. They test where they start, build a calendar with rest days in it, log every session, adjust the plan on day 15, then test again on day 30 the exact same way.
need: A calendar page or a notebook page with 30 squares
A timer, and a tape measure or a phone for distances
Shoes that fit, and a safe place for the goal: a yard, a park, a pool with a lifeguard
Coloured pencils for the plan and the graph

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: Expect a flat-out first day and a slump by day five unless the plan has rest built in. Set your limits before they choose anything, count the tests yourself, and guard the rest days as closely as the training days.

plan.what: Pick the goal, test the start and build the calendar (Steps 1 to 3).
Train, log and adjust at day 15 (Step 4).
Test again the same way and compare (Step 5).

troubleshoot.q: It's too easy by week two
troubleshoot.a: That's what the day-15 check is for. Add a set or a harder version, like full push-ups instead of knee push-ups, rather than extra training days.
Use the Sore or hurt card together. Sharp pain or a sore joint means stop and rest, and if it's still there in a few days, ask a doctor. The plan waits.

troubleshoot.q: Their goal is about how they look
troubleshoot.a: Turn it into something the body does, like a longer run or a stronger hold. Never weigh or measure their body for this guide; the numbers are reps, seconds and metres.

lesson.text: Muscles, heart and lungs get stronger in the rest after the work, not during it. A plan that starts below your best, adds a little each week and leaves rest days in between beats going all out every day, and it's far less likely to end in an injury.
lesson.before: 'I'll do as many as I can every day until I get there.'

model.line: 6 push-ups with good form, counted by a grown-up.
3 sets of 3, three days a week, 1 more per set each week.
9 push-ups. Most sessions felt like working, so the plan stayed.
After an easy day 29: 14 push-ups, same rule, same time.

lesson.modelNote: 'As many as I can every day' left no time to rebuild. Sets of half the start number, rest days and a check halfway turned 6 into 14, and the same counting rule on both days proves it.

steps.title: Pick a goal your body can do
steps.why: A goal with a number can be tested on day 30. A goal about looks can't, and isn't the point.
steps.kid: Your kid picks one thing they want their body to do in 30 days, like run 2 km without stopping, hold a plank for a minute or swim a length, and checks it against the Goal check card in the Training Plan Toolkit at the end of the guide. They write the goal as one sentence with a number in it.
steps.you: Set your limits first: where they can train, and what needs you there, like pools, roads or anything upside down. Steer any goal about weight or looks toward something the body does.
ask: How will we know on day 30 that you did it?
Is this hard now, but possible in a month?
steps.tip: One goal, not three. One plan is easier to follow and to measure.

levels.explore: Pick something to do by the end of the month, like a cartwheel, and show a parent your first try.
levels.develop: Write the goal with a number, and check it against every line of the Goal check card.
levels.extend: Pick a goal that needs two things, like distance and speed, and decide which one to train first and why.

steps.title: Test where you start
steps.why: Without a start number, day 30 has nothing to compare with.
steps.kid: Your kid warms up, then does one honest test using the Start test card: the most push-ups with good form, the longest plank, or how far they run before they have to walk. First they write the rule for what counts as one, so day 30 is judged the same way.
steps.you: Count or time it yourself, and stick to the rule they wrote. Keep it light: this number is a starting point, not a score.
ask: What counts as one, and what doesn't?
What would make the day-30 test unfair?
steps.tip: Write down the time of day, the place and the shoes. Day 30 should match all three.

levels.explore: Try it once while a parent counts or times, and colour in your start number.
levels.develop: Write the rule, do the test, and record the number with the time, place and shoes.
levels.extend: Test on two different days, and decide which number is your true start, and why.

steps.title: Build the 30 days
steps.why: A plan that adds a little and rests often beats going all out every day.
steps.kid: Your kid draws 30 squares and fills them in using the Build-up rules card: training days, rest days, a check on day 15, an easy day 29 and the retest on day 30. They pick a starting practice from the Sample plans card, then write how much they'll add each week.
steps.you: Check the plan with them: a rest day after each hard one, and no big jumps. Agree when training happens, so it fits your real days.
ask: Why does day 29 need to be easy?
How much will you add each week?
steps.tip: Three or four training days a week is plenty. More days doesn't make a better plan.

levels.explore: Colour training days one colour and rest days another on a calendar, with a parent.
levels.develop: Fill in all 30 squares with what to do on each training day.
levels.extend: Predict your day-30 number from what you'll add each week, and write it in the day-30 square now.

steps.title: Train, log and adjust
steps.why: The log shows whether the plan fits the body, and day 15 is where good planners change it.
steps.kid: On each training day, your kid does the plan and writes one line using the Log and adjust card: what the plan said, what they really did, how hard it felt and how their body feels. On day 15 they do a mini test, read the log and decide: add, hold or ease off.
steps.you: Train alongside them when you can, with a goal of your own. If they mention pain, go through the Sore or hurt card together, and make the call on stopping yourself.
ask: Were most sessions easy, working or all out?
What does your day-15 number say about the plan?
steps.tip: Missed a day? Pick up where the calendar is. Don't double up to catch up.

levels.explore: After each practice, tell a parent if it felt easy, okay or hard, and draw a face for it.
levels.develop: Log every training day, and change the plan on day 15 if the log says to.
levels.extend: Note one thing outside training beside each log line for a week, like sleep or a busy day, and see if it matches how sessions felt.

steps.title: Test again on day 30
steps.why: The same test, done the same way, is the only fair way to know if the plan worked.
steps.kid: After an easy day 29, your kid repeats the start test with the same rule, time, place and shoes. They put day 1, day 15 and day 30 on a simple graph, compare it with their prediction, and write in a notebook what they'd keep and change for the next 30 days.
steps.you: Count with the same rule you used on day 1, even if it costs them one. Then celebrate the planning, whatever the number.
ask: How far did you come from day 1?
What would you change in the next plan?
steps.tip: Short of the goal? The graph still shows how far they came. Keep the plan and push the retest two weeks later.

levels.explore: Do the test again while a parent counts, and put your day 1 and day 30 numbers side by side.
levels.develop: Retest, graph your three numbers, and write what you'd keep and change.
levels.extend: Work out how much you gained per week, and use it to set a fair goal and date for a different skill.

conclusion.headline: They trained for a month and can prove what worked.
conclusion.text: Pick a goal of your own for the next 30 days and ask them to build your plan. If they start by testing you and leave you rest days, they understood the plan, not only the push-ups.
conclusion.celebrate: When they put the day-1 and day-30 numbers side by side, say: 'You built that number yourself, one planned day at a time, rest days included.'
extensions: Train a parent or a sibling for 30 days using a plan they write
Pick a new goal in a different area, like balance after strength, and build a fresh plan
Find out how a real athlete in a sport they like plans the week before a race, and compare it with their day 29
Swap one training day a week for a new activity, like swimming for a runner, and see what the log shows

signs: They ask 'what counts?' before measuring anything
They take rest days without feeling guilty
They change a plan because of what the numbers say
makeItReal: Ask your kid at dinner what one thing they wish their body could do by next month, then do the start test together tomorrow.

classroom.intro: A whole class can train for 30 days together, each student toward their own goal, during gym or a daily movement break. The testing, calendar and log are the same for everyone, so it runs smoothly.

tips.d: Offer goals that fit your space and supervision: a plank, a wall sit, push-ups, a skipping streak or a run around the field. Swimming goals only happen in supervised lessons.
Pair students for the start test. One counts with the written rule while the other does it, then they swap. Day 30 uses the same partner, time of day, place and shoes.
Thirty days include weekends and holidays, so mark those as rest days or home sessions. Avoid starting right before a long break, or day 15 and day 30 land when nobody's at school.
Steer every goal toward something the body does, never weight or appearance. Logs and numbers stay private, and nobody compares scores out loud.
Teach the Sore or hurt card on day one. Anyone with sharp pain or a sore joint stops and tells you, and students with health limits get an adapted goal.
A face drawn after each practice works for the youngest. Most log every session and adjust on day 15. Extend students predict day 30 and work out their weekly gain.

classroom.timing: Day 1 takes one 45-minute session for goals, start tests and calendars. Training fits 10 to 15 minutes, three or four days a week. Day 30 brings retests and graphs. Students can add weekend sessions at home.
